mainHtml:
Dialysis Clinic Cleaning Services

Support for dialysis units where blood exposure is routine: station-area environmental cleaning, spill response and end-of-day terminal cleaning, all documented.

Environmental cleaning for outpatient dialysis

Hemodialysis is one of the few outpatient settings where contact with blood is routine. Dialysis facilities that participate in Medicare follow the infection control condition for coverage in 42 CFR 494.30, which points to CDC's recommendations for preventing transmission of infections among chronic hemodialysis patients. Environmental cleaning is part of that picture, alongside the clinical steps your team owns.

Between treatments vs. end of day

CDC's dialysis guidance calls for the station — chair, side tables, the external surfaces of the machine — to be cleaned and disinfected after the patient leaves and before the next patient is seated. In most units the patient care technicians perform that between-treatment clean. Our role is the environment around it and the full terminal clean after the last shift:

  • Terminal cleaning of every station area, floors under and around chairs, and the treatment floor.
  • Isolation areas used for patients with hepatitis B, cleaned with dedicated equipment as your policy requires.
  • Blood spill response with an EPA-registered disinfectant labelled for bloodborne pathogens, used at its full contact time.
  • Waiting rooms, scales, restrooms and staff areas — the places patients and staff touch before and after treatment.
  • Clean and soiled utility rooms kept separate, with no clean supplies stored where soiled items are handled.

What our team does not do

We do not reprocess dialyzers, touch water-treatment systems or handle sharps. Regulated medical waste stays with your licensed hauler under 105 CMR 480.000. Keeping those lines clear is part of an honest scope.

Related: bloodborne pathogen cleanup protocols and terminal vs. concurrent cleaning.

Request a Free Facility Assessment

Compliance, Certifications & Documentation

Massachusetts healthcare facilities are subject to multiple layers of regulatory oversight. Our cleaning protocols are designed to support your compliance program across:

  • Massachusetts Department of Public Health (DPH): 105 CMR 130 hospital licensure, 105 CMR 140 clinic regulations, 105 CMR 150 long-term care facilities, and the local board of health's inspection authority.
  • OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030): All staff complete annual bloodborne pathogen training before deployment to clinical environments.
  • CDC Environmental Infection Control Guidelines: Cleaning sequences, contact times, and hand hygiene protocols aligned with CDC HICPAC recommendations.
  • EPA-Registered Hospital-Grade Disinfectants: List N (SARS-CoV-2), List P (Candida auris), List H (MRSA and VRE) and List K (C. difficile) products applied with documented contact times.
  • HIPAA Privacy Awareness: Environmental services staff trained on patient privacy in clinical areas, including handling of materials that may contain protected health information.
  • Joint Commission & AAAHC Survey Support: Documentation, audit trails, and quality control reports formatted to support accreditation surveys.

ATP Bioluminescence Verification — Proof Your Facility Is Truly Clean

Visual inspection only confirms that surfaces look clean. ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate) bioluminescence testing measures the amount of organic residue on a surface in 10 seconds — providing objective, numerical proof of disinfection effectiveness. This is the same technology used by infection prevention programs in major U.S. hospitals.

We offer ATP verification testing as part of our standard quality control program. Pass/fail readings are logged for each tested surface, giving your facility documented evidence of cleaning effectiveness for accreditation surveys, internal quality reviews, and patient safety committees.

Most healthcare facilities in Massachusetts have never had their surfaces objectively verified — not because they don't care, but because nobody has offered them the technology. Until now.
